```{=html}
<div class="lab-head">
  <h2 class="lab-h"><span class="lab-n">1</span>One reading</h2>
  <a class="lab-skip" href="#ch2">I know this → skip</a>
</div>
<div class="lab-intro">
<div class="lab-intro-text">
<p class="lab-story">The thermometer shows a number. Let's give it a name.</p>
<details class="lab-ctx"><summary>Why does this matter?</summary><p>Every measurement is a number with a unit: 78.3 °C. Giving it a name (a variable) is the first step of every analysis, from a school lab to a space probe.</p></details>
<div class="lab-ask" data-right="2">
<p class="lab-q"><span class="lab-qm" aria-hidden="true">?</span><span>The tea reads 78.3 °C and the room 21 °C. Which number tells you how fast the tea is cooling right now?</span></p>
<div class="lab-opts" role="group" aria-label="Your guess">
<button type="button" class="lab-opt" data-opt="1" aria-pressed="false">78.3, the temperature of the tea</button>
<button type="button" class="lab-opt" data-opt="2" aria-pressed="false">57.3, how much hotter it is than the room</button>
<button type="button" class="lab-opt" data-opt="3" aria-pressed="false">21, the temperature of the room</button>
</div>
<button type="button" class="lab-justshow">I would rather just see it</button>
<p class="lab-reveal" hidden><strong class="lab-verdict"></strong> The hotter the tea is above the room, the faster it cools: that gap is what Newton's law is about. You just computed it: 57.3 °C.</p>
</div>
<p class="lab-bubble" hidden data-text="Try changing 78.3 to 40, then press Run Code."></p>
</div>
```

:::: {.lab-pair .lab-lazy}

```{pyodide}
from tealab import gauge     # a helper that draws a thermometer

T = 78.3      # ← try 40      the thermometer reading (°C)
gauge(T)
```

::::

```{=html}
<p class="lab-sub"><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M12 20h9M16.5 3.5a2.1 2.1 0 013 3L7 19l-4 1 1-4z"/></svg>Your turn</p>
<p class="lab-hint">Fill in the blank (<code>___</code>). Press Run Code.</p>
```

:::: {.lab-pair .lab-turn data-nudge="Replace ___ with a subtraction: the tea minus the room. Then press Run Code."}

```{pyodide}
T = 78.3          # tea (°C)
room = 21.0       # room (°C)

gap = ___         # ← how much hotter is the tea than the room?
print("gap =", round(gap, 1), "°C")
```

::::

```{=html}
<details class="lab-solution"><summary>Stuck? Show the answer</summary>
<pre><code>gap = T - room</code></pre></details>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lab-head">
  <h2 class="lab-h"><span class="lab-n">2</span>Many readings</h2>
  <a class="lab-skip" href="#ch3">I know this → skip</a>
</div>
<div class="lab-intro">
<div class="lab-intro-text">
<p class="lab-story">Every 15 seconds, one more reading. A row of numbers with one name is an array.</p>
<details class="lab-ctx"><summary>Why does this matter?</summary><p>A data set is a list of readings tied to time. A NumPy array does arithmetic on the whole list at once, which is why scientists use it instead of plain lists.</p></details>
<div class="lab-ask" data-right="2">
<p class="lab-q"><span class="lab-qm" aria-hidden="true">?</span><span>The tea starts at 78.2 °C and the last of 6 readings, 75 s later, is 62.9 °C. About how much did it cool in total?</span></p>
<div class="lab-opts" role="group" aria-label="Your guess">
<button type="button" class="lab-opt" data-opt="1" aria-pressed="false">About 5 °C</button>
<button type="button" class="lab-opt" data-opt="2" aria-pressed="false">About 15 °C</button>
<button type="button" class="lab-opt" data-opt="3" aria-pressed="false">About 40 °C</button>
</div>
<button type="button" class="lab-justshow">I would rather just see it</button>
<p class="lab-reveal" hidden><strong class="lab-verdict"></strong> 15.3 °C in 75 s, and you got it with T[0] - T[-1]. Keep the number: in the next chapters you will see that the cooling slows down.</p>
</div>
<p class="lab-bubble" hidden data-text="Change one of the readings and press Run Code. What changes?"></p>
</div>
```

:::: {.lab-pair .lab-lazy}

```{pyodide}
import numpy as np

t = np.array([0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 75])                  # time (s)
T = np.array([78.2, 74.9, 71.0, 68.6, 65.1, 62.9])     # ← change a reading   temperature (°C)

print("readings:", len(T))
print("first:", T[0], "  last:", T[-1])
print("mean:", T.mean())
```

:::: {.lab-pair .lab-turn data-nudge="Tip: Python counts from 0, so T[0] is the first reading. How would you reach the last one?"}

```{pyodide}
import numpy as np

T = np.array([78.2, 74.9, 71.0, 68.6, 65.1, 62.9])

drop = ___        # ← first reading minus last reading
print("the tea cooled by", round(drop, 1), "°C")
```

::::

```{=html}
<details class="lab-solution"><summary>Stuck? Show the answer</summary>
<pre><code>drop = T[0] - T[-1]</code></pre></details>
```

```{=html}
  <h2 class="lab-h"><span class="lab-n">3</span>See it</h2>
  <a class="lab-skip" href="#ch4">I know this → skip</a>
</div>
<div class="lab-intro">
<div class="lab-intro-text">
<p class="lab-story">Our eyes read a picture faster than a column of numbers.</p>
<details class="lab-ctx"><summary>Why does this matter?</summary><p>Look at your data before you compute anything. A graph shows in a second what a column of numbers hides: trends, outliers, mistakes.</p></details>
<div class="lab-ask" data-right="2">
<p class="lab-q"><span class="lab-qm" aria-hidden="true">?</span><span>Plot temperature against time. What shape do you expect?</span></p>
<div class="lab-opts" role="group" aria-label="Your guess">
<button type="button" class="lab-opt" data-opt="1" aria-pressed="false">A straight line going down</button>
<button type="button" class="lab-opt" data-opt="2" aria-pressed="false">A curve that flattens</button>
<button type="button" class="lab-opt" data-opt="3" aria-pressed="false">A curve that drops faster and faster</button>
</div>
<button type="button" class="lab-justshow">I would rather just see it</button>
<p class="lab-reveal" hidden><strong class="lab-verdict"></strong> A curve that flattens: fast while the tea is hot, slow when it is close to room temperature. A straight line would mean a constant cooling speed.</p>
</div>
<p class="lab-bubble" hidden data-text="Replace &quot;o&quot; with &quot;-&quot; and press Run Code."></p>
```

:::: {.lab-pair .lab-lazy}

```{pyodide}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from tealab import tea

t, T = tea()                       # 40 simulated readings of the cooling tea

plt.plot(t, T, "o")                # ← try "-" or "o-"
plt.xlabel("time (s)")
plt.ylabel("temperature (°C)")
plt.show()
```

```{=html}
<div class="lab-head">
  <h2 class="lab-h"><span class="lab-n">4</span>Wobble</h2>
  <a class="lab-skip" href="#ch5">I know this → skip</a>
</div>
<div class="lab-intro">
<div class="lab-intro-text">
<p class="lab-story">Read the same temperature twice and you get two numbers. The typical gap between them is σ (sigma).</p>
<details class="lab-ctx"><summary>Why does this matter?</summary><p>Every instrument wobbles. σ, the standard deviation of repeated readings, is how a physicist puts a number on that wobble. It is the error bar in your lab report.</p></details>
<div class="lab-ask" data-right="1">
<p class="lab-q"><span class="lab-qm" aria-hidden="true">?</span><span>Drag the wobble σ to the right. What do you expect to see?</span></p>
<div class="lab-opts" role="group" aria-label="Your guess">
<button type="button" class="lab-opt" data-opt="1" aria-pressed="false">Longer bars and more scattered points</button>
<button type="button" class="lab-opt" data-opt="2" aria-pressed="false">Fewer points on the graph</button>
<button type="button" class="lab-opt" data-opt="3" aria-pressed="false">A different shape of the curve</button>
</div>
<p class="lab-reveal" hidden><strong class="lab-verdict"></strong> The bars are ± σ: more wobble, longer bars, more scatter. The curve behind the points does not change. And repeated readings give you σ: your 30 readings of the bath came out close to the true 0.4 °C.</p>
</div>
<p class="lab-bubble" hidden data-text="Drag the slider to the right and watch the bars."></p>
```

:::: {.lab-pair .lab-turn data-nudge="Tip: a NumPy array can tell you its own spread. One word, then ()."}

```{pyodide}
import numpy as np
from tealab import noise_series

T = 50 + noise_series(30, 0.4)     # 30 readings of a bath kept at 50 °C (true wobble: 0.4)

sigma = T.___()                    # ← one word: the spread of the readings (standard deviation)
print("sigma =", round(sigma, 2), "°C")
```

::::

```{=html}
<details class="lab-solution"><summary>Stuck? Show the answer</summary>
<pre><code>sigma = T.std()</code></pre></details>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lab-head">
  <h2 class="lab-h"><span class="lab-n">5</span>Fit</h2>
  <a class="lab-skip" href="#ch6">I know this → skip</a>

<div class="lab-intro">
<div class="lab-intro-text">
<p class="lab-story">Newton: the gap between tea and room shrinks by the same fraction every second. Python finds the one number that matters: τ.</p>
<details class="lab-ctx"><summary>Why does this matter?</summary><p>Newton's law of cooling says the gap to the room shrinks by the same fraction in equal times. The same exponential describes a discharging capacitor, radioactive decay, and caffeine leaving your blood.</p></details>
<div class="lab-ask" data-right="2">
<p class="lab-q"><span class="lab-qm" aria-hidden="true">?</span><span>Set the cooling time to 400 s: the tea cools more slowly. What will the fit find?</span></p>
<div class="lab-opts" role="group" aria-label="Your guess">
<button type="button" class="lab-opt" data-opt="1" aria-pressed="false">About 240 s, the default</button>
<button type="button" class="lab-opt" data-opt="2" aria-pressed="false">About 400 s, within its ±</button>
<button type="button" class="lab-opt" data-opt="3" aria-pressed="false">Something random</button>
</div>
<button type="button" class="lab-justshow">I would rather just see it</button>
<p class="lab-reveal" hidden><strong class="lab-verdict"></strong> The fit finds the τ the tea really had, within its ±. That is what fitting is for. Now use it: how long until the tea is drinkable?</p>
</div>
```

```{pyodide}
#| echo: false
#| autorun: true
#| input:
#|   - cooling_time
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import curve_fit
from tealab import tea, show

t, T = tea(0.4, 15, cooling_time)

def model(t, Ta, T0, tau):
    return Ta + (T0 - Ta) * np.exp(-t / tau)

par, cov = curve_fit(model, t, T, p0=[20, 80, 100])
show(t, T, 0.4, model, par, cov, residuals=False)
```

```{pyodide}
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import curve_fit
from tealab import tea, show

def model(t, Ta, T0, tau):                              # Newton's law of cooling
    return Ta + (T0 - Ta) * np.exp(-t / tau)

noise = 0.4          # ← try 1.5     wobble of each reading (°C)
t, T = tea(noise)

par, cov = curve_fit(model, t, T, p0=[20, 80, 100])     # p0: a first guess for Ta, T0, tau
tau = par[2]
d_tau = np.sqrt(cov[2, 2])                              # the uncertainty of tau
print(f"tau = {tau:.0f} ± {d_tau:.0f} s")
show(t, T, noise, model, par, cov, residuals=False)
```

::::

```{=html}
<p class="lab-sub"><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M12 20h9M16.5 3.5a2.1 2.1 0 013 3L7 19l-4 1 1-4z"/></svg>Your turn</p>
<p class="lab-hint">Use the fit to predict. Fill in the blank (use <code>np.log</code>). Press Run Code.</p>
```

:::: {.lab-pair .lab-turn data-nudge="Tip: solve the equation for t by taking the logarithm of both sides. np.log is the natural log."}

```{pyodide}
import numpy as np
from tealab import tea, newton_fit

t, T = tea()
Ta, T0, tau = newton_fit(t, T)       # the fit from the cell above, in one call

t60 = ___      # ← seconds until the tea reaches 60 °C: solve 60 = Ta + (T0 − Ta)·exp(−t/τ) for t
print(f"The tea is at 60 °C after {t60:.0f} s")
```

::::

```{=html}
<details class="lab-solution"><summary>Stuck? Show the answer</summary>
<pre><code>t60 = -tau * np.log((60 - Ta) / (T0 - Ta))</code></pre></details>
```

:::: {.lab-pair .lab-lazy}

```{pyodide}
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import curve_fit
from tealab import tea, show

laws = {
    "newton": lambda t, Ta, T0, tau: Ta + (T0 - Ta) * np.exp(-t / tau),
    "almost": lambda t, Ta, T0, tau: Ta + (T0 - Ta) / (1 + t / tau),
    "wrong":  lambda t, Ta, T0, tau: Ta + (T0 - Ta) * np.exp(-(t / tau) ** 2),
}
model = laws["newton"]    # ← try "almost", then "wrong"

noise = 0.4
t, T = tea(noise)

par, cov = curve_fit(model, t, T, p0=[20, 80, 100],
                     sigma=np.full(t.size, noise), absolute_sigma=True, maxfev=5000)
show(t, T, noise, model, par, cov)
```

::::

```{=html}
<p class="lab-sub"><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M12 20h9M16.5 3.5a2.1 2.1 0 013 3L7 19l-4 1 1-4z"/></svg>Your turn</p>
<p class="lab-hint">Compute the number behind the light. Fill in the blank. Press Run Code.</p>
```

:::: {.lab-pair .lab-turn data-nudge="Tip: square each residual with ** 2, then add them up with np.sum."}

```{pyodide}
import numpy as np
from tealab import tea, newton_fit

noise = 0.4
t, T = tea(noise)
Ta, T0, tau = newton_fit(t, T)
fit = Ta + (T0 - Ta) * np.exp(-t / tau)

residuals = (T - fit) / noise        # how many σ each point is from the curve
chi2 = ___                           # ← add up the squares of the residuals
print("reduced chi2 =", round(chi2 / (t.size - 3), 2))    # about 1 = the fit agrees with the bars
```

::::

```{=html}
<details class="lab-solution"><summary>Stuck? Show the answer</summary>
<pre><code>chi2 = np.sum(residuals ** 2)</code></pre></details>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lab-wrapup">
  <p class="lab-can"><strong>Now you can</strong> tell a good fit from a bad one: the residuals look like noise and the reduced χ² is about 1 (green).</p>
  <p class="lab-because" style="margin:0;opacity:.85;max-width:26rem">The fit looks good. But is the ± it reports honest? Repeat the experiment and see.</p>
  <a class="lab-next" href="#ch7"><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M12 5v14M6 13l6 6 6-6"/></svg>7 · Repeat</a>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lab-head">
  <h2 class="lab-h"><span class="lab-n">7</span>Repeat</h2>
  <a class="lab-skip" href="#ch8">I know this → skip</a>
</div>
<div class="lab-intro">
<div class="lab-intro-text">
<p class="lab-story">Do the experiment again, and again. If the fit's ± is honest, τ scatters by about that much. Real noise often has memory: each reading remembers the one before.</p>
<details class="lab-ctx"><summary>Why does this matter?</summary><p>Repeating a virtual experiment many times, to see how the result scatters, is called a Monte Carlo. When you cannot repeat the real experiment a hundred times, the computer can.</p></details>
<div class="lab-ask" data-right="2">
<p class="lab-q"><span class="lab-qm" aria-hidden="true">?</span><span>The fit says τ = 240 ± 3 s. Repeat the experiment 100 times when the noise has memory 0.9. How much does τ really scatter?</span></p>
<div class="lab-opts" role="group" aria-label="Your guess">
<button type="button" class="lab-opt" data-opt="1" aria-pressed="false">About ± 3 s, as the fit says</button>
<button type="button" class="lab-opt" data-opt="2" aria-pressed="false">About ± 6 s, twice as much</button>
<button type="button" class="lab-opt" data-opt="3" aria-pressed="false">About ± 30 s, ten times as much</button>
</div>
<button type="button" class="lab-justshow">I would rather just see it</button>
<p class="lab-reveal" hidden><strong class="lab-verdict"></strong> About twice as much. With memory the fit's ± is too optimistic, even though τ is still right on average.</p>
</div>
<p class="lab-bubble" hidden data-text="Set memory = 0.9 and press Run Code."></p>
</div>
```

:::: {.lab-pair .lab-lazy}

```{pyodide}
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import curve_fit
from tealab import tea, spread

noise = 0.4      # ← try 1        wobble of each reading (°C)
memory = 0.0     # ← try 0.9      0 = none, near 1 = each reading remembers the one before
repeats = 100    # ← try 300      how many times we repeat the experiment

def model(t, Ta, T0, tau):
    return Ta + (T0 - Ta) * np.exp(-t / tau)

taus, claimed = [], []
for k in range(repeats):
    t, T = tea(noise, memory=memory, seed=k)
    par, cov = curve_fit(model, t, T, p0=[20, 80, 100],
                         sigma=np.full(t.size, noise), absolute_sigma=True)
    taus.append(par[2])
    claimed.append(np.sqrt(cov[2, 2]))

spread(taus, claimed)
```

::::

```{=html}
<p class="lab-challenge"><strong>Challenge.</strong> Which memory makes the fit overconfident by a factor 2? The fit gets τ right on average. What does it get wrong?</p>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lab-head">
  <h2 class="lab-h"><span class="lab-n">8</span>Noise</h2>
  <a class="lab-skip" href="#end">I know this → skip</a>
</div>
<div class="lab-intro">
<div class="lab-intro-text">
<p class="lab-story">Noise is not only how much. It can have memory. Look at the residuals, then at your own data.</p>
<details class="lab-ctx"><summary>Why does this matter?</summary><p>Real instruments have inertia and drift, so one reading remembers the last. When that happens, averaging N readings helps less than the usual σ/√N promises.</p></details>
<div class="lab-ask" data-right="1">
<p class="lab-q"><span class="lab-qm" aria-hidden="true">?</span><span>In the residuals, the chip shows r₁, how much each value resembles the one before. If the noise were pure chance, what would r₁ be?</span></p>
<div class="lab-opts" role="group" aria-label="Your guess">
<button type="button" class="lab-opt" data-opt="1" aria-pressed="false">About 0</button>
<button type="button" class="lab-opt" data-opt="2" aria-pressed="false">About 1</button>
<button type="button" class="lab-opt" data-opt="3" aria-pressed="false">About 0.5</button>
</div>
<p class="lab-reveal" hidden><strong class="lab-verdict"></strong> About 0, within ± 2/√N. The sample data show r₁ = +0.75: the wobble has memory, so the ± of a plain fit is too optimistic.</p>
</div>
<p class="lab-bubble" hidden data-text="Drag memory to 0.9."></p>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<button type="button" class="lab-i" aria-expanded="false" aria-label="What is memory?">i</button>
```

```{=html}
<button type="button" class="lab-i" aria-expanded="false" aria-label="What is the thermometer step?">i</button>
<p class="lab-info" hidden>A digital thermometer shows steps, not every value. With a big step the histogram turns into teeth; the rounding alone adds a wobble of about step/√12.</p>
```

```{pyodide}
#| echo: false
#| autorun: true
#| input:
#|   - memory
#|   - thermo_step
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import curve_fit
from tealab import tea, look

noise = 0.4
t, T = tea(noise, memory=memory, step=thermo_step)

def model(t, Ta, T0, tau):
    return Ta + (T0 - Ta) * np.exp(-t / tau)

par, cov = curve_fit(model, t, T, p0=[20, 80, 100],
                     sigma=np.full(t.size, noise), absolute_sigma=True)
look(t, T, noise, model, par, cov)
```

:::: {.lab-pair .lab-turn data-nudge="Tip: paste your own lines in place of the sample, and keep the first line, t,T."}

```{pyodide}
import io
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import curve_fit
from tealab import look

data = """t,T
0,80.1
20,74.6
40,69.6
60,65.3
80,60.9
100,57.5
120,54.2
140,51.7
160,49.4
180,47.4
200,45.4
220,43.3
240,41.6
260,40.3
280,38.4
300,37.1
320,35.7
340,34.9
360,33.4
380,32.3
400,31.5
420,30.7
440,29.4
460,28.9
480,28.3
500,27.7
520,27.2
540,26.9
560,26.0
580,26.2
"""            # ← paste your own measurements here: time (s), temperature (°C)

t, T = np.loadtxt(io.StringIO(data), delimiter=",", skiprows=1, unpack=True)

def model(t, Ta, T0, tau):
    return Ta + (T0 - Ta) * np.exp(-t / tau)

par, cov = curve_fit(model, t, T, p0=[20, T[0], 100])
sigma = np.std(T - model(t, *par), ddof=3)         # the wobble, estimated from the data itself
look(t, T, sigma, model, par, cov)
```

```{=html}
<p class="lab-hint">If the chip is amber or red, the wobble of your data has memory: the ± of the fit is too optimistic.</p>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lab-wrapup">
  <p class="lab-can"><strong>Now you can</strong> read the noise in real data: how much it wobbles, whether it has memory, and what that does to the uncertainty.</p>
  <p class="lab-because" style="margin:0;opacity:.85;max-width:26rem">That is the whole path.</p>
```

```{=html}
  <ol>
    <li>Store a measurement in a variable and calculate with it.</li>
    <li>Keep many readings in an array and ask it questions.</li>
    <li>Turn numbers into a graph with labelled axes.</li>
    <li>Measure the wobble σ of a reading.</li>
    <li>Fit a law, read τ ± its uncertainty, and predict with it.</li>
    <li>Judge a fit with the residuals and the reduced χ².</li>
    <li>Repeat an experiment on the computer to test the uncertainty.</li>
    <li>Read the noise in real data: wobble and memory.</li>
  </ol>
  <p>Want to go deeper? Play with the noise itself: its memory, the thermometer step, and how much averaging really helps.</p>

</section>
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Words

- **variable**: a name for a value, like `T = 78.3`.
- **array**: many values in a row, with one name.
- **σ (sigma), noise, wobble**: how much one reading can be off. The bars on the points.
- **fit**: finding the numbers that bring a curve closest to the data.
- **cooling time (τ, tau)**: how fast the tea cools. Larger means slower.
- **residual**: data minus fit, point by point.
- **χ² (chi-squared)**: around 1 (green) the fit agrees with the bars; higher (amber, red) something is off.
- **memory (autocorrelation)**: how much a noise value resembles the one before.
- **repeat (Monte Carlo)**: do the experiment many times on the computer and look at the scatter of the result.
- **function, lambda, dictionary**: a recipe with inputs; a tiny unnamed recipe; a labelled collection like `laws["newton"]`.
:::
